planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; this species flowers one to two weeks before common lilac, so site it where an early frost is unlikely to damage the first flush of buds.

directions: Native to northern China, Syringa oblata is one of the earliest lilacs to bloom and was later used as a parent of the Hyacinthiflora hybrid lilacs bred for cold climates and early flowering. Its broad, almost kidney-shaped leaves are wider than they are long, distinguishing it at a glance from common lilac, and in many strains the foliage turns an unusual wine-red to purple in autumn, a trait rare among lilacs. Fragrant lavender-purple flower panicles are shorter and denser than those of Syringa vulgaris, opening on old wood while the garden is still mostly bare. Give it a real winter chill and full sun for best bloom, and prune out a portion of the oldest stems after flowering to keep the multi-stemmed shrub from becoming congested.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early spring or fall in well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun; thin a few of the oldest canes after bloom each year to keep the naturally arching habit from becoming a dense thicket.

directions: First raised in France in the late 1700s as a chance hybrid between Syringa × persica and Syringa vulgaris, the Rouen lilac combines the fine-textured, narrower leaves of Persian lilac with the fuller, more fragrant flower trusses of common lilac. Its slender, gracefully arching branches become smothered in reddish-purple panicles slightly earlier in the season and more reliably every year than most common lilac cultivars, since it blooms heavily even on younger wood. The smaller, finer-textured foliage gives it a lighter, airier look in the border than the coarser-leaved French hybrid lilacs. It is notably resistant to the powdery mildew that often disfigures common lilac foliage by late summer.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted stock in spring in average, well-drained soil; some direct sun deepens the purple leaf color, but afternoon shade helps in hot climates where foliage can scorch.

directions: Chameleon spurge is grown for its smoky purple-bronze foliage, which darkens through the growing season and sets off the small chartreuse-and-maroon flower clusters that open in late spring. It spreads gently by shallow rhizomes and seeds itself freely; because seedlings can vary from the deep purple of the parent toward plainer green, shearing off spent flower stalks before seed drops keeps a patch looking uniform. Like all spurges its milky latex sap can irritate skin and eyes, so wear gloves when dividing or cutting it back. It combines well with silver or chartreuse-leaved companions in a shaded border and tolerates fairly poor, dry soil once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun; prune lightly right after flowering since blooms form on old wood, and avoid heavy watering once the plant is established.

directions: Native across Siberia, Mongolia, and northern China, Spiraea trilobata is a tidy, rounded shrub with small blue-green, three-lobed leaves that look more like a currant's foliage than a typical spirea's. In late spring it covers itself in dense, rounded clusters of small white flowers strung along the previous year's wood, giving a neat mounding display similar to 'Snowmound' but on a noticeably hardier, more drought-tolerant plant. It shrugs off harsh winters and dry, alkaline soils better than most Japanese spirea selections, making it a good choice for prairie and high-plains gardens. Light shaping right after bloom is all the pruning it needs to keep its naturally compact, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; stake young trees loosely for the first year and prune to a strong scaffold structure while the wood is still young and pliable.

directions: Crataegus × prunifolia 'Splendens' is a tough, broad-leaved hawthorn hybrid grown for its glossy foliage that turns burgundy-orange in fall and its heavy crop of persistent red haws that often hang on well into winter. Compared with typical cockspur thorn it carries noticeably fewer, shorter thorns, making it easier to site near walkways and patios while still giving birds the dense, thorny branching they use for nesting cover. Clusters of white flowers open in late spring ahead of the fall fruit display, and the tree tolerates urban pollution, compacted soil, and drought once established, which has made it a popular street and parking-lot tree. Prune while young to establish well-spaced scaffold branches, since the dense wood heals slowly once the tree matures.
